title: Gauss-Wilson Theorem: Product of Units and Cyclic Groups
description: Formalizes the Gauss-Wilson theorem: ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic, proved via involution lemma and self-inverse classification. Full proof that cyclic → product = -1 and non-cyclic → product = 1. Verifies Gauss-Wilson for all n ≤ 300 and confirms no Wilson primes between 14 and 100. 20 theorems, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: The Gauss-Wilson theorem originated in Gauss's Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801): the product of all units mod n equals -1 exactly when (ℤ/nℤ)* has a primitive root — equivalently when (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic — which occurs iff n ∈ {1,2,4,p^k,2p^k} for odd prime p. The proof strategy — pairing group elements with their inverses — is a classical argument: non-self-inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) cancel, leaving only the self-inverse elements (those with x² = 1). For cyclic groups this set is {1, -1}, giving product = -1. For non-cyclic groups the self-inverse elements form an elementary abelian 2-group of size ≥ 4, forcing the product to 1. Formalizing this in Lean requires Finset.prod_involution (the pairing lemma), IsCyclic.card_pow_eq_one_le (the cyclic group cardinality bound), and the concrete-abstract bridge via Finset.prod_nbij. The non-cyclic case is handled in a companion file WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext using a fixed-point-free involution with constant pair product.
overview.problemStatement: For which n is ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 (mod n)? Prove it equals -1 iff (ℤ/nℤ)* is cyclic, using the involution pairing lemma.
overview.text: The key proof is the involution lemma: in any finite abelian group G, pair each element with its inverse. Elements not equal to their inverse cancel in pairs. The remaining product is ∏{x | x²=1}. In a cyclic group with n≥3, the only self-inverse elements are 1 and -1, so ∏{x | x²=1} = -1. In a non-cyclic unit group, there exists a Klein-four subgroup, and the product of a Klein-four group is 1, making the total product 1. This gives the complete characterization.
overview.proofStrategy: Prove the involution lemma: ∏G = ∏{x : x²=1} via Finset.prod_involution. Prove cyclic unit groups have exactly {1,-1} as self-inverse elements using IsCyclic.card_pow_eq_one_le + sandwich. Prove non-cyclic case via WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext. Combine for the biconditional. Bridge to concrete unitsProduct via Finset.prod_nbij.
keyInsights: Involution product lemma: non-self-inverse pairs (a, a⁻¹) cancel via Finset.prod_involution; ∏G reduces to ∏{x | x²=1}
Cyclic sandwich: |{x|x²=1}| ≤ 2 (IsCyclic) and {1,-1} ⊆ {x|x²=1} with -1≠1, so {x|x²=1} = {1,-1} exactly
Non-cyclic: the self-inverse set forms an elementary abelian 2-group of size ≥ 4, handled by WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext via fixed-point-free involution
Concrete-abstract bridge: unitsProduct_cast_eq_abstract via Finset.prod_nbij with bijection x ↦ ZMod.val(x)
The proof is purely group-theoretic: independent of the specific ring structure of ℤ/nℤ
Computational confidence: gaussWilson_verified_le_300 and no Wilson primes in [14,100] verified by native_decide
prerequisites: Finite abelian groups: Finset.prod_involution, pairing with inverses
Klein-four group: elementary abelian 2-groups and their products

conclusion.summary: Gauss-Wilson theorem proved abstract and concrete: ∏(ℤ/nℤ)* = -1 ↔ IsCyclic (ZMod n)ˣ, via involution product lemma, self-inverse classification in cyclic groups, Klein-four argument for non-cyclic case, and Finset.prod_nbij bridge. Computationally verified for n ≤ 300; no Wilson primes in [14, 100]. 20 theorems, 8 definitions, 462 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: The Gauss-Wilson theorem is the algebraic foundation for primitive root theory: (ℤ/nℤ)* cyclic iff primitive roots exist mod n, characterizing the n where the discrete logarithm is well-defined. The involution product lemma is a general technique applicable to any finite abelian group product computation. The companion WilsonsTheoremOQ02Ext provides the non-cyclic case via a fixed-point-free involution with constant pair product — a technique applicable beyond this setting.
openQuestions: Are there infinitely many Wilson primes? Equivalent to: are there infinitely many p with p | B_{p-1}?
